### 1. Data and source

Our data come from two public sources. The first is the results database of ClinicalTrials.gov. The files in data/raw/ctgov describe phase III and phase II/III studies from the registry. studies.csv lists the studies, arms.csv their arms and hazard_ratios.csv the hazard ratios (HR) they post for progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). The second is HemOncKB, a knowledge base of cancer drugs and regimens hosted on the Harvard Dataverse. We use its release of August 28, 2026 (version 54) for the drug classes and the drug synonyms.

The script code/build_data.R keeps each study that posts an HR with a two-sided 95% confidence interval (CI) for PFS and for OS on the same two groups. When a study posts several such comparisons it takes the first one posted. It then codes each arm as containing an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) or not with the drug names and synonyms of HemOncKB, plus a few short forms such as Pembro. An arm is read from its title. Its description is used only when the title says nothing. Placebo, supportive care and observation arms count as arms without an ICI. An ICI that only shows up in a description can be crossover after progression. These comparisons stay undetermined. The tumor type comes from the conditions field, or from the study title when the conditions are too vague. The result is saved in data/processed/trials_first_pass.csv.

```{r}
source("../code/build_data.R")
nrow(studies)
table(studies$allocation)
table(studies$phases)
nrow(trials)
table(trials$phase)
```

The registry files hold 2290 studies, all randomized. Out of them, 526 have such a comparison and 12 of those are phase II/III. For these 12 we will check in the manual review that the results come from the phase III part. As planned in the proposal we keep solid tumors only.

```{r}
sum(trials$tumor == "hematologic")
solid = trials[trials$tumor != "hematologic", ]
solid$log.os = log(solid$os.hr)
solid$log.pfs = log(solid$pfs.hr)
solid$se.os = (log(solid$os.upper) - log(solid$os.lower))/(2*1.96)
nrow(solid)
```

This drops 83 hematologic comparisons and leaves 443. We define $Y_i$ as the log HR for OS, $X_i$ as the log HR for PFS and $s_i = (\log U_i - \log L_i)/(2 \cdot 1.96)$ as the approximate standard error of $Y_i$, where $(L_i, U_i)$ is the 95% CI of the OS HR. When an HR is posted as experimental against control, a value below 1 favors the experimental arm. In the code the three variables are log.os, log.pfs and se.os.

Our work so far is a first automatic pass and nobody has reviewed the records manually yet. In particular we don't know yet if the ICI arm is always the experimental one. The HRs are also taken as posted, without checking their direction.

### 2. Data quality

```{r}
cont = solid[, c("log.os", "log.pfs", "se.os", "start.year")]
cont.tab = data.frame(missing = colSums(is.na(cont)),
                      non.missing = colSums(!is.na(cont)),
                      mean = apply(cont, 2, mean),
                      median = apply(cont, 2, median),
                      sd = apply(cont, 2, sd),
                      IQR = apply(cont, 2, IQR))
round(cont.tab, 3)
```

No continuous variable has missing values, since the code only keeps HRs that come with both CI limits. The median log HR is $-0.236$ for PFS and $-0.105$ for OS. We can see that effects on OS are closer to 0 and less spread out (sd 0.238 for OS against 0.383 for PFS). The median start year is 2015 and the IQR is 9 years.

```{r}
mean(solid$log.pfs > 0)
mean(solid$log.os > 0)
```

The PFS HR is above 1 in 21% of the comparisons and the OS HR in 26%. An HR above 1 can mean that the experimental arm did worse. It can also mean that the trial posted the HR the other way round (control against experimental). The manual review will tell which.

```{r}
sum(solid$n.pairs > 1)
sum(solid$pfs.n.hr > 1 | solid$os.n.hr > 1)
```

In 53 studies there is more than one PFS-OS comparison. In 194 there are several HRs for the same end point and the same arms, for instance in subgroups. The code keeps the first one posted. It can be a subgroup rather than the primary analysis. The manual review will pick the primary comparison and analysis, with PFS and OS in the same population.

```{r}
w = 1/solid$se.os^2
round(range(solid$se.os), 3)
max(w)/min(w)
low = order(solid$se.os)[1:3]
solid[low, c("nct.id", "os.hr", "os.lower", "os.upper", "se.os")]
solid$arm1[low]
solid$arm2[low]
```

The standard error se.os goes from 0.044 to 1.220. With weights $w_i = 1/s_i^2$, the most precise comparison weighs about 785 times more than the least precise one. We take a closer look at the three comparisons with the smallest se.os, as they weigh the most. The first one (NCT02178956) posts an OS HR of 1.01 with a CI from 0.86 to 1.02. On the log scale a Wald CI is centered on the log HR. Here the HR sits almost on the upper limit. The trial paper gives 0.86 to 1.20 (Shah et al., Clin. Cancer Res. 2022). The registry entry swaps two digits (1.02 for 1.20). We will correct it in the manual review. The second one compares darbepoetin alfa (a drug for anemia) with placebo. The proposal only keeps comparisons of anticancer drugs. This one goes. The manual review will also look for other supportive care trials. The third (NCT03675737) looks fine.

```{r}
asym = (log(solid$os.upper) + log(solid$os.lower))/2 - log(solid$os.hr)
solid[abs(asym) > 0.05, c("nct.id", "os.hr", "os.lower", "os.upper")]
```

More generally, a gap above 0.05 between a log HR and the middle of its CI on the log scale flags 4 comparisons, NCT02178956 included. Rounding can explain one of them (NCT00631371 posts 1.0 with 0.9 to 1.3). We will check the other two against the publications.

```{r}
cat.vars = solid[, c("ici.status", "tumor")]
data.frame(missing = colSums(is.na(cat.vars)),
           non.missing = colSums(!is.na(cat.vars)))
table(solid$ici.status)
options(width = 76)
table(solid$tumor)
```

Neither categorical variable has missing values. For ici.status this is only because the code labels unclear comparisons as undetermined. We will code these 42 in the manual review. Out of the 443 comparisons, 114 are coded as having an ICI in one arm only and 256 in no arm. The proposal excludes the 31 with an ICI in both arms, since their control arm has one. One can observe that lung is by far the most common tumor type (135) and pancreas the rarest (10).

### 3. Overlap of the two groups

The first step of our plan is to check whether the 114 ICI comparisons and the 256 non ICI ones overlap in tumor type, PFS effect and start year.

```{r}
analysis = solid[solid$ici.status %in% c("ICI in one arm", "no ICI"), ]
nrow(analysis)
tab = table(analysis$tumor, analysis$ici.status)
tab
round(prop.table(tab, 2), 2)
```

Breast cancer is 6% of the ICI group but 18% of the non-ICI group. Gastroesophageal (12% vs 5%), head and neck (9% vs 4%) and liver or biliary tumors (8% vs 3%) are more than twice as frequent among ICI comparisons. Pancreas has 10 non-ICI comparisons and no ICI one. Melanoma and other have only 2 ICI comparisons each. So the tumor mix differs between the 2 groups.

```{r, fig.height = 3}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), las = 1)
boxplot(log.pfs ~ ici.status, data = analysis, xlab = "",
        ylab = "log HR for PFS")
boxplot(start.year ~ ici.status, data = analysis, xlab = "",
        ylab = "start year")
```

```{r}
tapply(analysis$log.pfs, analysis$ici.status, median)
tapply(analysis$log.pfs, analysis$ici.status, min)
```

The median log HR for PFS is $-0.198$ in the ICI group and $-0.274$ in the other. The lowest ICI value is $-1.05$. The non-ICI ones go down to $-1.90$. So the PFS effects overlap over most of the range.

```{r}
tapply(analysis$start.year, analysis$ici.status, median)
period = cut(analysis$start.year, c(1997, 2008, 2013, 2022),
             labels = c("1998-2008", "2009-2013", "2014-2022"))
table(period, analysis$ici.status)
```

The median start year is 2017 for ICI comparisons against 2011 for the others. In this first pass no ICI comparison started before 2009. Only 6 started between 2009 and 2013 against 94 non-ICI ones. One can observe that start years overlap much less than PFS effects. Even with start year in the model, part of the non-ICI slope would come from years without any ICI comparison. A restriction on period or on clinical setting could help but it would also change the two other checks. We will decide on it after the manual review and before the final fit.

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
plot(log.os ~ log.pfs, data = analysis, las = 1,
     xlab = "log HR for PFS", ylab = "log HR for OS")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 2)
abline(0, 1)
```

This plot pools the two groups. Most points sit in the lower left quadrant (where both HRs are below 1). The association is positive but the cloud is flatter than the solid line of slope 1. We can see that OS effects vary less than PFS effects (as in section 2).

### 4. Hypothesis and baseline model

We hypothesize that the trial-level slope linking the treatment effect on OS to the treatment effect on PFS differs between ICI and non-ICI comparisons. Let $I_i = 1$ if only the experimental arm of comparison $i$ contains an ICI and $I_i = 0$ if neither arm does. Let $Z_i$ hold the tumor type and the start year. The baseline model is the model from our proposal
$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \beta_2 I_i + \beta_3 X_i I_i + \gamma^\top Z_i + \varepsilon_i$$
fitted by weighted least squares with weights $w_i = 1/s_i^2$. The model assumes that the slopes do not vary with tumor type or start year. Then $\beta_1$ is the PFS-OS slope without an ICI and $\beta_1 + \beta_3$ the slope with an ICI, for a given tumor type and start year. We test
$$H_0\colon \beta_3 = 0 \quad \text{against} \quad H_A\colon \beta_3 \neq 0$$
Under $H_0$ the two groups share the same PFS-OS slope. We report the estimate of $\beta_3$ with a 95% CI. Both the CI and the test use heteroscedasticity-consistent (sandwich) standard errors in the HC3 form. HC3 corrects for leverage. The comparisons with very large weights (section 2) have high leverage. Weighted least squares assumes that the variance of $Y_i$ is proportional to $s_i^2$. This fails if trials also vary by an extra amount on top of their sampling error. The sandwich standard errors do not rely on this assumption. With them the t distribution is only an approximation.

As a baseline we fit the model to the 370 comparisons of section 3, before the manual review and before any restriction.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
```

```{r}
analysis$ici = as.numeric(analysis$ici.status == "ICI in one arm")
fit = lm(log.os ~ log.pfs * ici + tumor + start.year, data = analysis,
         weights = 1/se.os^2)
hc = vcovHC(fit, type = "HC3")
round(coeftest(fit, vcov = hc)[c("log.pfs", "ici", "log.pfs:ici"), ], 3)
round(coefci(fit, vcov = hc)["log.pfs:ici", ], 3)
round(sum(coef(fit)[c("log.pfs", "log.pfs:ici")]), 3)
round(summary(fit)$sigma, 2)
```

The estimated slope is 0.355 without an ICI and 0.468 with one. So $\hat\beta_3 = 0.113$, with a 95% CI from $-0.031$ to 0.257 and a p-value of 0.12. At the 5% level we can't reject $H_0$. The CI still allows a much steeper slope in the ICI group, as well as a slightly flatter one. Both slopes are well below 1, in line with the flat cloud of section 3.

The residual standard error of the weighted fit is 1.2. If $s_i$ were the only source of variation it would be close to 1. So the comparisons vary more than their sampling errors imply. Part of this can come from the errors of section 2. If the extra variation does not scale with $s_i^2$, the model-based standard errors are off. The sandwich ones still hold.

These numbers are only a baseline. The manual review will correct HRs (such as NCT02178956), drop comparisons that are not of anticancer drugs and code the 42 undetermined ones. Section 3 also showed that the two groups barely overlap in start year and that pancreas has no ICI comparison. So the adjustment for $Z_i$ partly relies on extrapolation. We will decide on a restriction from the overlap checks only and refit the model once, together with the residual, Cook's distance and unweighted checks of the proposal.
